title: My solo Solana memecoin system is now averaging 4.44 SOL/day live. Here's everything I wish someone had told me.
author: West-Following2465
selftext:
For 15 months, the thing that scared me most wasn't losing money. It was becoming a statistic.

You know the ones. Three out of four retail crypto investors lose money. Most memecoin traders get wiped out. Every time I opened my laptop, part of me wondered if I was just writing a slower, more expensive version of the same story: a guy who gave up more than a year of his life to join the 75%.

I'm a solo developer. I've spent the last 15 months building MCHPai, an autonomous Solana memecoin trading system. Over the past few weeks of live mainnet trading it has averaged 4.44 SOL a day. That's a short sample, and I'm not taking a victory lap. But I'm not a statistic yet, and I want to tell you what it took: the numbers, the parts nobody posts, and the advice I wish someone had handed me on day one.

The statistics I was afraid of joining

About three-quarters of retail bitcoin app users lost money on their bitcoin (73% to 81% across 95 countries, 2015–2022). Source: BIS.

Over 60% of active Pump.fun traders lost money over six months. That's out of about 4.26 million wallets. Only about 5,000 (roughly 0.1%) made over $100K, and only 311 (under 0.01%) made over $1M. Source: Dune, June 2025.

Only 0.4% of about 13.5 million Pump.fun wallets had locked in more than $10K in profit. Source: Dune, January 2025.

98.6% of the 7M+ tokens launched on Pump.fun showed signs of rug pulls or pump-and-dumps. Source: Solidus Labs, May 2025.

Those numbers aren't abstract when your savings and your evenings are on the line. They're the thing you think about at night.

What it cost in dollars

Claude Max 20x (for Claude Code), 18 months: $3,600

Helius Business data feed, 6 months: $2,994

Trading capital lost while learning: $3,000

Cash total: about $9,600

That's the cheap part. I worked 4 to 12 hours a day, 6 days a week, for 15 months, which comes to 1,560 to 4,680 hours. I normally earn about $55 an hour. Every hour I spent on this was an hour I wasn't getting paid, and the bills didn't care about my thesis. That's $85,800 to $257,400 in wages I gave up, which puts my true cost between about $95,000 and $267,000. More than 90% of it is time.

What it cost in everything else

Here's the part nobody posts.

There were nights I seriously thought about walking away. Not "this is frustrating." More like "I'm done." Over those 15 months I watched $3,000 of real money disappear. I walked away from 13 versions of one bot and a 95,000-line codebase I'd been proud of. I also found out that two of my safety checks had never run, because a free-tier API had been quietly rejecting requests since deployment. Nothing crashed, and nothing warned me.

It's lonely. Nobody around me really got what I was building. Try explaining "I'm modeling trader psychology on Solana memecoins" to someone outside this world and watch their eyes glaze over.

My relationships took a hit too: family, friends, my social life. When you're putting in up to 12 hours a day, six days a week, something gives, and it's usually the people who deserve your time the most.

Under all of it was the money stress, and that one question: what if I'm wrong? What if I give up all this time and money and come out the other side as just another wallet in a Dune dashboard?

What kept me going was simple. I wanted a better life. I wanted to stop trading hours for wages. At about $121 per SOL, 4.44 SOL a day is roughly $537. That's about what I'd earn in 10 hours at my old rate. It's not freedom yet. But it's the first time this thing has looked like the door I've been trying to build.

If you're going to do this, protect the human first

Decide your quit criteria before you start: a dollar limit, a date and a metric. Then the decision gets made by you with a clear head, not by you at your lowest point. Know your runway, meaning exactly how many months of bills you can cover without income, because money stress makes you take trades and shortcuts you shouldn't. Tell the people in your life what you're doing and why, and protect your time with them the way you'd protect a production deploy. Find people who get it, whether that's a community like this one or one friend who builds things. The isolation is real, and it warps your judgment. And take at least one day off a week. Exhausted builders make sloppy risk decisions, and in this market sloppy gets expensive fast.

The gut check: 15 signs you're built for this

If you see yourself in most of these, I think you should try it. A few of them I had to earn the hard way.

You can grind without applause. Most months will have nothing to show anyone.

You can kill your darlings. Sunk cost is the most expensive bug in this game.

You trust evidence over excitement. New ideas wait until the data catches up.

You refuse to fake it. No mock data, no guessed inputs, no "close enough."

You're a little obsessive about verification. Every change gets tested and can be undone.

You think in systems, not trades. You naturally see the whole pipeline: signal, processing, action.

You're curious about data nobody's processing well. That curiosity beats any indicator.

You're willing to have your own thesis. If you're running what Crypto Twitter runs, you're their exit liquidity.

You respect risk more than you love winning. Boring safeguards keep you alive.

You can wear every hat. Developer, data engineer, ops and risk manager. Solo means all of it.

You treat losses as tuition, not something to win back.

You put real numbers on your goals. "Make money" isn't a goal.

You use AI as a force multiplier, not a crutch. Let it write fast, then make it prove the code works.

You document like future-you is a stranger. Because they will be.

You can sit with doubt without letting it drive. You'll feel like quitting. Feel it, then go check the data.

The playbook

1. Find your edge before you write code. Why would you win against the person on the other side of the trade? Speed, better information, better reading of behavior, or better discipline. Mine is behavior: on memecoins, the chart is mostly a side effect of people, so I model the people. If you can't answer that in one sentence, you're not ready to trade real money. You're ready to collect data. Pick one slice of the market and get great at it first.

2. Treat data as the real product. Record everything to disk from day one, including the tokens that die. Otherwise survivorship bias will make every strategy look better than it is. Cross-check your main feed against a second source, and build alerts that fire the moment data stops flowing. Silent failures are the ones that hurt you.

3. Build boring models first. Start with a dumb baseline and a simple model before any neural net. My rug filter is still a plain logistic regression. Include fees in your definition of a win. Test walk-forward with a gap between training and test data, and never shuffle time series. Hunt down any feature that peeks into the future. Make sure the model's confidence matches reality: if it says 70%, those trades should win about 70% of the time. Train offline first, then fine-tune live.

4. Respect execution. Paper trading flatters everyone. Measure the real gap: latency, slippage and failed transactions. Tight stops with fast re-entries will chop you to death on fees. Give trades room, add cooldowns, and exit when the reason you entered stops being true.

5. Make risk and security non-negotiable. Give the bot its own capped hot wallet, and never put your main key on a server. Set per-trade caps, a daily loss limit and a kill switch. When anything breaks, the system should hold instead of trading. Before every buy, check for live mint authority (the creator can print more supply) and freeze authority (the creator can lock your tokens). Also check holder concentration and whether insiders can pull liquidity.

6. Don't fool yourself. Change one thing at a time. Write a post-mortem on every trade. Don't trust a strategy until it has a few hundred trades behind it across different conditions, and that includes my 4.44 SOL/day. Be skeptical of everyone's P&L screenshots, mine included.

7. Handle the boring adult stuff. In the US, every swap is a taxable event because the IRS treats crypto as property. A bot can make thousands of trades a year, so log your cost basis from day one and talk to a tax pro early. Not tax advice.

So, should you build one?

If you read this and saw yourself in it, the traits and the struggles too, I think you should. The tools have never been this good for one person with an idea and the stubbornness to see it through. You might end up a statistic. That risk is real, and I felt it every single week. But you might not. I'm 15 months in, and so far I'm not one.

If you didn't see yourself in that list, that's not a verdict. It's a to-do list.

What this means for me, and why I think now is the time

If this holds, it changes my life. Not in a Lambo way. In a quiet way. It means the hours I put in finally buy my freedom instead of being sold off at $55 a pop. It means paying back what this cost me, in dollars and in time, and giving that time back to the people who waited on me while I built it. It means waking up and choosing what to build next instead of asking someone else what I'm worth this week. 

And the thing I keep coming back to is how new this is. Not long ago, a solo developer with a home PC had no real shot at building something like this. That took a funded team. Today one stubborn person with an AI coding partner, a real-time data feed and open, permissionless markets that never close can build it, ship it and run it. We're living in a window of opportunity most people don't realize is open, and I don't know how long it stays this wide. 

So if you've been sitting on an idea, whether it's a trading system or anything else, this is your sign. Take the risk seriously, protect your people, and go build the door you want to walk through.

Happy to answer questions in the comments, about the build or about the grind. I won't share exact signals or settings. Not financial advice. Memecoins are brutal, and a few good weeks don't change that.

TL;DR: About 75% of retail crypto investors lose money, and over 60% of active Pump.fun traders do too. I spent 15 months, about $9,600 in cash and $86K–$257K in forfeited wages, fighting not to become one of them. It cost me relationships, money stress and nearly my resolve. 

It's now averaging 4.44 SOL/day over a few weeks live. If it holds, it's my way out of trading hours for wages, and I think we're living in a rare window where one person can build something like this. Protect your runway and your people, find your edge, start on paper, and if you fit the gut check, go build it.

replies.author: West-Following2465
replies.body:
Here's what you'd be walking into. Solidus Labs flagged about 98.6% of tokens launched on pump.fun as rug pulls or pump-and-dumps. Of the 7M+ tokens launched there, only about 97k still had even $1,000 of liquidity. Most memecoins go to zero, and fast.

If you still want to learn (and it's smart that you're asking first), this is what I'd do:

Only trade money you'd be fine losing completely. Think of your first deposit as tuition.

Use a separate wallet just for trading. Never share your seed phrase, never sign anything from a link in DMs or Telegram, and ignore anyone who says they're "support."

Check a token before you buy it (RugCheck or similar):

mint and freeze authority are revoked
liquidity is locked or burned
the top holders don't own a big chunk of the supply
the dev didn't bundle buys at launch


Learn how bonding curves, slippage, liquidity and MEV/sandwich bots work. Not understanding these is how people lose on trades that "should" have worked.

Set your exit rules before you buy, like taking your initial out at 2x. Most losses come from riding a pump all the way back down.

Log every trade: entry, exit, size and why you took it. After 50+ trades you'll know whether you have an edge or just got lucky once.

The real edge here is tools, data and discipline, not a secret note. At 19, learning to code (Python or TypeScript)

comments.author: Jesse_daone
comments.body:
This is awesome, very well done and hope the best for you and your bot 🙏. 

I'm about 10 months into building a Solana Telegram-first automated trader, so your comment about killing 13 versions and a 95k-line codebase hit pretty close to home.
My mechanical side is finally near the point where I want to freeze it: multi-source/caller capture, deterministic paper decisions, fail-closed health, restart/reconciliation, execution telemetry and a research/export layer. I'm trying hard not to spend another six months “perfecting plumbing” before focusing on behavior.
Without sharing any of your proprietary signals/settings: what objective criteria told you your mechanical/execution layer was finally “done enough” to stop rebuilding it and move on? And looking back at those 13 versions, what 2–3 things did you realize you had over-engineered or simply did not need?
Also, when you say behavior became your edge, I'm curious about categories rather than thresholds: did you get more value from participant/actor behavior, source/caller timing, or post-entry/exit behavior? Which data categories turned out not to be worth the engineering cost?

replies.author: West-Following2465
replies.body:
Thanks, and good luck with yours. That's a solid list for 10 months in.

When was the plumbing "done enough"?

For me it came down to three checks:

Every failure is loud. One bug changed my mind on this. Jupiter's free tier rejected a quote parameter I was sending with HTTP 400, and that quietly switched off two of my protection modules from the day they shipped. Nothing crashed; they just did nothing. After that I added cross-feed verification, and "no silent failures" became the bar.

I can measure the paper-to-live gap. Once I had tooling that showed how far paper fills drift from what live would have gotten, paper results meant something, and I could stop rebuilding.
The apparatus is ahead of the evidence. I set a hard rule: no new modules until the evidence catches up with the apparatus. If your instrumentation collects more than you're analyzing, the plumbing is done.

To actually freeze it, I version-tag and hash-verify every build. That way "just one tweak" has to pass the same test battery as a new feature.

What I over-engineered or didn't need:

The ML stack. The old version was 95k lines with 42 models across 6 tiers. The rug filter I ship now is a plain logistic regression (0.885 AUC on 499 clean mints).

Feature breadth. I capture 174 features, but most of the value comes from a small core.
Caller/social data. For me it wasn't worth the engineering cost. Since you're Telegram-first, I'd test that early before building more around it.

UI/dashboards, and building things for problems I didn't have yet.

Where the edge came from

It's less glamorous than a category: data, and more of it. I mean volume and coverage of clean data, not more features. For example, 93.6% of mints had never been seen on the bonding curve by my feed, and the ones I'd tracked from the curve priced about 7× cleaner. Save everything raw (I moved from in-memory to DuckDB/Parquet) so you can ask new questions of old data later.

The other edge was the audacity to believe AI could push my skills past where they were. I'd submit my current models, ask for brutal, constructive feedback, and build on that, over and over.

One last thing: new ideas go straight into paper trading, but nothing touches real money until it clears evidence gates.
